notes.meaning: Paul instructs masters to treat their slaves with justice and fairness. In the ancient world, masters held total power, but Paul reminds them that they also answer to a Master in heaven. God treats everyone without favoritism, so Christian masters must care for those under them with equity and kindness. Remembering God's authority over us helps us treat others fairly.

Believers are told to make prayer a regular, steady habit. They must stay spiritually alert, keeping their minds focused and watching for how God is working. Every prayer should also be filled with thanksgiving for God's blessings. Staying watchful and thankful keeps our prayer lives fresh and active.

Paul asks the church to pray specifically for him and his fellow workers. He does not ask for an easy release from prison, but for God to open a door of opportunity to preach the gospel. Even while locked in chains, his greatest desire was sharing the good news about Christ. We can support God's ministers by praying for their work.

Paul asks for prayer so that he will declare the message of Christ clearly and boldly. Proclaiming God's truth is a serious duty, and he wanted to preach it exactly as God commanded. He knew that human words alone cannot save, so he relied on God's Spirit to make the truth clear to his hearers.

Christians must act with wisdom and care toward outsiders who do not yet believe. Their everyday conduct should never give people an excuse to look down on the gospel. Believers are told to buy up every opportunity they have to do good and show God's love to those around them.

Our everyday speech should always be pleasant, gracious, and helpful. Just as salt adds good flavor to food and stops it from going bad, gracious words keep talk wholesome and appealing. Speaking with wisdom prepares Christians to give a thoughtful answer to anyone who asks about their faith.

Paul sends Tychicus to deliver the letter and give a full report on his situation. Tychicus was a trusted Christian brother from Asia who served faithfully alongside Paul. By calling him a fellow servant, Paul shows that all believers are equal partners in the Lord's work.

Paul sent Tychicus on this long journey so the Colossians would know how he was doing and be encouraged. Learning that Paul remained joyful and steadfast in prison would bring comfort to their hearts. Christian fellowship gives us strength when we hear how other believers remain faithful through hard times.

Traveling with Tychicus was Onesimus, a native of Colossae who had previously run away from his master Philemon. After meeting Paul and placing his faith in Christ, Onesimus was returning home as a dearly loved Christian brother. God's grace can change a person completely and give them a brand-new standing in God's family.

Aristarchus, who shared Paul's imprisonment in Rome, sends his greetings to the church. Paul also mentions Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and tells the believers to welcome him warmly if he visits. Though Paul and Mark had once separated over a past failure, they were now reconciled and serving together in love.

A believer named Jesus, also known by the Roman name Justus, sends his greetings as well. Paul notes that Justus, Mark, and Aristarchus were the only Jewish believers working beside him in Rome for God's kingdom. Their loyal companionship brought great personal comfort and encouragement to Paul in his trials.

Epaphras, who had first brought the gospel to Colossae, sends his love to the congregation. Even while far away in Rome, he constantly wrestled in deep, passionate prayer for them. His great longing was for these believers to stand spiritually mature and completely settled in God's will.

Paul gives personal witness to how hard Epaphras worked in his heart for the Colossian believers. His deep concern also reached the nearby towns of Laodicea and Hierapolis in the Lycus Valley. Epaphras loved these flocks and labored to keep them safe from misleading teachings.

Luke, the doctor who wrote the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts, sends his warm greetings. Paul also passes along greetings from Demas, another coworker who was with him at the time. Luke's medical care and faithful friendship were a rich comfort to Paul during his imprisonment.

Paul sends greetings to the Christian brothers and sisters living in nearby Laodicea. He gives special honor to Nympha and the group of believers who met in that home for worship. In the first centuries, churches did not have special buildings, so believers gathered in private houses.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars and translations identify the host as a woman named Nympha, based on the earliest Greek manuscripts that read 'her house.'

notes.meaning: Paul gives instructions that this letter be read aloud to the whole Colossian church and then sent to Laodicea. In return, the Colossians were to obtain and read the letter coming from Laodicea. Sharing letters between local congregations helped the early churches remain unified in true Christian teaching.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: While some early writers believed the letter from Laodicea was a personal letter that was later lost, many scholars think it was a circular letter meant for several churches, such as the letter to the Ephesians.

notes.meaning: Paul directs the congregation to pass along an encouraging charge to Archippus. He was to take great care to finish the ministry the Lord had entrusted to him. Serving God is a lifelong calling that requires steady faithfulness and dedication.

Paul takes the pen from his secretary to write the final greeting with his own hand to show the letter is genuine. He asks the believers to remember his chains in their prayers and leaves them with the blessing of God's grace. His willingness to suffer for the truth showed how deeply he believed the message he preached.
